blocks.title: Wavefront
blocks.text: A wavefront is an imaginary surface joining all the points where the waves have the same phase.

items: Plane wavefronts: represented by straight lines, like light from distant stars and water waves in a ripple tank.
Circular wavefronts: represented by circles, as formed on water in a pond.
Spherical wavefronts: formed in three-dimensional space by a sound or light wave from a point source.

blocks.text: For a point source in space the wavefronts are spherical, spreading out in all directions. At very large distances, as for light from the Sun, a small part of such a wavefront can be treated as a plane. The shortest distance between successive wavefronts is one wavelength, and the energy of the wave always travels at right angles to the wavefront. A line at right angles to a wavefront showing its direction of travel is called a ray. A line source such as a vibrator in a ripple tank gives plane wavefronts; a point source gives circular wavefronts in two dimensions and spherical ones in three. A source of light placed at the focal point of a lens gives plane wavefronts on the other side of the lens. This chapter uses plane wavefronts to study interference and diffraction.

blocks.alt: Three panels. Plane: parallel vertical blue lines with a red ray crossing them at right angles. Circular: concentric blue circles around a red point source, with red arrows pointing outward. Spherical: arcs of increasing radius spreading from a point source along a red ray; the far arcs are almost straight.
blocks.caption: Plane, circular and spherical wavefronts (original diagram after Fig 15.1).
blocks.long_description: Rays always cross wavefronts at right angles. Far from a point source the wavefronts are so large that the part we see is practically flat.
